title: Normalised bank transaction
description: THE SCHEMA IS DATA, NOT CODE, and that is deliberate. The same corpus has to serve the Python implementation and the TypeScript implementation without either one becoming the reference: two implementations that each carry their own truth drift apart, and that is how this kind of project dies. The measurement behind this file (2026-08-05): on the same notion of a transaction, the mt940 library returns 37 fields and ofxparse returns 10, with only THREE fields in common (amount, date, identifier). The counterparty is called applicant_name on one side and payee on the other.

date.description: The date the statement line itself carries, and the one to sort and reconcile by. Its provenance differs by format and saying so is more honest than pretending otherwise: MT940 field :61: value date, OFX DTPOSTED. Calling it the value date, as this schema did before 0.1.0, was wrong for OFX, where DTPOSTED is the posting date and the closest thing to a value date is DTAVAIL, which most files omit.

booking_date.description: A second date, when the format supplies one the BANK set: MT940 entry date, OFX DTAVAIL (funds availability). Null otherwise. It never holds a date the customer set, such as OFX DTUSER, which lives in `raw`: a date whose meaning is not recorded is a plausible wrong answer.

amount.description: DECIMAL AS A STRING, never a float. A cent lost inside a binary64 is a false reconciliation, and the source format already carries exact decimals.

currency.description: Nullable, and the corpus is what made it so. A real file (ofxparse issue #81, two Australian banks) carries an EMPTY CURDEF, and the rule for that case says to keep the transaction and leave the currency unset. Dropping the entry instead would reject a whole statement over one empty tag, and guessing a currency from the country or the bank identifier would produce the wrong-but-plausible figure this project exists to avoid.

check_number.description: The cheque number. It earns a field of its own because the corpus has a case where it is the ONLY identifying content of the transaction (LCL, a CHECK with no NAME and no MEMO), and because two upstream sources spell its tag differently, CHECKNUM and CHKNUM. Kept as a string: leading zeros are significant.

raw.description: ALWAYS present. The fields specific to the source format, as they are. A normalisation that throws away the original forces you to re-parse the file as soon as a question falls outside the schema, and nobody keeps the file.
